standard.title: Characteristics of Australia's Democracy
standard.description: the characteristics of Australia's democracy, including freedom of speech, association, assembly, religion and movement
standard.prior_knowledge: Students know key values and beliefs of Western democracies (AC9HS6K06) and can identify roles and responsibilities of different levels of government (AC9HS6K07). They understand that Australia's government emerged from Federation and is grounded in constitutional arrangements (AC9HS6K01, AC9HC7K01).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the characteristics of Australia's democracy, including democratic freedoms and how they support active participation, and identify limits on these freedoms.

nodes.label: Democratic freedoms
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the key democratic freedoms in Australia — freedom of speech, association, assembly, religion and movement — and their role in enabling democratic participation.
nodes.minimum_width: Name the five key democratic freedoms and explain in general terms why each is important for people to participate in democracy.
nodes.typical_width: Explain each of the five democratic freedoms (speech, association, assembly, religion, movement) and give examples of how each supports active participation in Australia's democracy — including voting, protest, community organising, and religious practice.
wider: Compare the protection of democratic freedoms in Australia with a country that has a formal bill of rights, exploring what difference constitutional protection makes
Examine historical cases in Australia where democratic freedoms have been contested or restricted, such as wartime censorship or Cold War anti-communist legislation
Investigate how Australia's democratic freedoms compare with international human rights frameworks such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding the five freedoms as a connected set is foundational — without clarity on what each freedom is and why it matters, subsequent nodes about limits on freedoms and active citizenship have no base. Students who treat freedoms as a list to memorise rather than as principles will not be able to reason about why limits exist.

response_modes.reason: Students need a clear repertoire of the five freedoms with concrete examples of each — building this range is the foundation before reasoning about limits and participation.

success_criteria: Name the five democratic freedoms and explain the role of each in enabling participation in democracy
Give a concrete example of how one freedom supports active civic participation

nodes.label: Limits on democratic freedoms
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain that democratic freedoms are not absolute and can be limited 'within the bounds of law', and identify reasons why such limits exist.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain that democratic freedoms can be limited by law and give at least one example of a legal limit on a freedom and the reason for it (e.g. defamation law limits freedom of speech to protect individuals).
nodes.typical_width: Explain that democratic freedoms are subject to legal limits and identify examples of how the law limits freedoms of speech, association, assembly, religion and movement; explain the reasons for such limits (e.g. protecting others' rights, national security, public order).
wider: Investigate a specific legal case where freedom of speech was tested in Australian courts, examining how courts balance competing rights
Explore how the limits on democratic freedoms in Australia compare with formal constitutional protections in other countries

Examine First Nations Australians' experience of legally enforced limits on freedoms (e.g. historical restrictions on movement under Protection Acts) and how this shapes understanding of democratic freedom

response_modes.reason: The concept of freedoms that are simultaneously protected and limited requires careful reasoning — students need to understand why a freedom can be both real and bounded, and what makes a legal limit legitimate rather than arbitrary.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Historical cases of legally enforced restrictions on First Nations Australians (Protection Acts, restrictions on movement) provide deeply significant context for understanding what it means when freedoms are absent — this makes the concept of democratic freedom genuinely meaningful rather than abstract.
success_criteria: Explain that democratic freedoms can be limited by law and identify at least one reason why such limits exist
Give an example of a legal limit on a democratic freedom and explain the purpose of that limit

nodes.label: Ways of participating in democracy
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and compare different ways citizens can participate in Australia's democracy, including formal and informal mechanisms.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least three ways citizens can participate in Australia's democracy (e.g. voting, petitioning, joining community organisations) and explain what each involves.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and describe a range of formal and informal participation mechanisms — voting, standing for parliament, contributing to parliamentary inquiries, petitions, social media campaigns, protest, volunteering, and community organisations — and compare their effectiveness for different purposes.
wider: Compare the effectiveness of different participation methods for specific civic goals (e.g. changing a law vs raising awareness vs influencing local decisions)
Investigate how digital tools and social media have changed the landscape of civic participation, including both new opportunities and risks
Examine examples of participation by young people and First Nations Australians, exploring what barriers and enablers exist for different groups

response_modes.reason: Students benefit from encountering the full range of participation forms — not just voting — to understand democracy as an ongoing practice rather than a periodic event.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Comparing participation methods for specific civic goals is genuinely productive — students who reason about which mechanism fits which purpose develop a much richer understanding of democratic agency than those who just list options.
success_criteria: Identify at least three ways citizens can participate in Australia's democracy
Explain why some forms of participation might be more effective than others for a given civic goal

nodes.label: Formal and active citizenship
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish between formal citizenship (legal status) and active citizenship (engaged participation), and identify who has been included and excluded from citizenship rights in Australia, particularly in relation to First Nations Australians.
nodes.minimum_width: Distinguish formal citizenship (legal membership of the nation, with associated rights) from active citizenship (engaged participation in civic life); identify that not all people in Australia have always had equal citizenship rights.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the attributes of formal and active citizenship; identify how First Nations Australians and other groups have been excluded from full citizenship rights and freedoms historically, and examine examples of First Nations Australians' active citizenship and advocacy (e.g. Neville Bonner, Adam Goodes, Noel Pearson, Ellie Gaffney).
wider: Investigate the 1967 referendum and the campaign leading to it as a case of active citizenship driving constitutional change

Examine the contributions of specific First Nations Australian citizens (Neville Bonner, Adam Goodes, Noel Pearson, Murundoo Yanner, Charles Mene, Ellie Gaffney, Evelyn Scott, Pat O'Shane) and the significance of their advocacy
Explore what it means to 'become' an Australian citizen through naturalisation, and what rights and responsibilities this confers

response_modes.reason: The exclusion of First Nations Australians from citizenship rights is not background information — it is central to understanding what Australian democracy has meant in practice. These cases must be substantively engaged with, not mentioned in passing.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The stories of First Nations Australian citizens who advocated for rights despite systemic exclusion offer rich opportunities to understand what active citizenship looks like under adversity — these are among the most significant and pedagogically powerful cases in the Australian civics curriculum.
success_criteria: Distinguish formal citizenship from active citizenship and explain what each involves
Identify that not all people in Australia have historically had equal access to citizenship rights, with reference to First Nations Australians
